overview.summary: Geologists study the Earth, its rocks, minerals, water and natural processes such as earthquakes and volcanoes, to understand the planet and to find and manage its resources.
overview.problems: They help find water and minerals, assess natural hazards such as landslides, and guide construction and environmental protection.
overview.worksWith: Engineers, mining and energy companies, environmental agencies, planners, other scientists and local communities.
overview.workplaces: Field sites, mines, quarries, laboratories, universities, government surveys and consultancies.

timeline.title: Planning fieldwork
timeline.description: The geologist studies maps and earlier reports and prepares equipment and safety plans.
timeline.why: Good planning makes field days safe and productive.

timeline.title: Fieldwork
timeline.description: The geologist walks the site, examines rock outcrops, takes measurements and collects samples.

timeline.title: Mapping and notes
timeline.description: The geologist records what was seen and marks it on maps.
timeline.why: Accurate records let others use the findings.

timeline.title: Laboratory or analysis
timeline.description: The geologist studies samples and data.
timeline.why: Tests show what the eye cannot.

timeline.title: Reports and advice
timeline.description: The geologist writes reports for clients or agencies and explains risks and options.
timeline.why: Decisions about land and resources depend on clear advice.

timeline.title: Remote work
timeline.description: Some jobs involve camping, long travel or work at mines and drill sites.
timeline.why: Geology happens where the rocks are.

responsibilities: Studying rocks, soil, water and landforms
Following safety rules on field sites
challenges: Fieldwork can be physically demanding, remote and in harsh weather.
Many jobs are tied to mining and energy, which move with market conditions.
Hazards include unstable ground, heat and machinery.
Projects can mean time away from home.
Much time goes on reports and data.
Competition for some roles is strong.
Some roles need a master's degree.
workEnvironment: A mix of outdoor fieldwork, laboratories and offices. Fieldwork can be in remote places and in all weather, sometimes at mines or construction sites. Office work includes mapping, analysis and reports.
rewards: Contributing to safety and resource management
tradeoffs: Pay that varies by country and industry

activity.title: Study rocks you can find safely
steps: With an adult, collect three small loose stones from a garden or a safe public area where collecting is allowed.
Describe each one: colour, texture, weight and whether you can see grains.
Compare them with pictures on a trusted geological survey website.
Draw a simple table of your findings and guess what each might be.
Note whether noticing small details felt interesting.
activity.outcome: You practise careful description and comparison, the first step in identifying rocks.
activity.safety: Do not hit or break rocks, do not visit cliffs, quarries, mines or riverbanks, and take stones only where collecting is allowed. Wash your hands afterwards.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
